summary.en: US authorities have taken a fugitive businessman into custody in Venezuela on bribery charges while Maduro and Cilia Flores face formal US accusations of ordering torture, sparking protests. An aid worker describes shocking earthquake damage in Venezuela and Rubio urges all opposition figures to join talks with the government. Starlink internet is now permitted to operate in Venezuela, and Cuba’s grid collapse is worsening regional strain on energy supplies. Energy firms are recruiting former US officials to access Venezuelan oil, and charges allege a PDVSA plane was used to transport goods.
summary.nb: US-myndighetene har tatt en flyktning forretningsmann i forvaring i Venezuela på bestikkelsesanklager mens Maduro og Cilia Flores står overfor formelle amerikanske anklager om å ha beordret tortur, noe som har utløst protester. En hjelpearbeider beskriver sjokkerende jordskjelvskader i Venezuela og Rubio oppfordrer alle opposisjonsfigurer til å delta i samtaler med regjeringen. Starlink-internett er nå tillatt å operere i Venezuela, og Cubas strømbrudd forverrer regionalt press på energiforsyningen. Energibedrifter rekrutterer tidligere amerikanske tjenestemenn for å få tilgang til venezuelansk olje, og anklagene hevder at et PDVSA-fly ble brukt til å transportere varer.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
